title: Minutes Until the Mold Spreads
statement:
A bakery tray is a grid grid. Each cell is 0 (empty), 1 (a fresh bun) or 2 (a moldy bun). Every minute, mold spreads from each moldy bun to every fresh bun that shares a side with it (up, down, left or right). All moldy buns spread at the same time. Mold cannot cross an empty cell or a corner.

Return the number of minutes until no fresh bun is left. If some fresh bun can never be reached, return -1. If there are no fresh buns at the start, the answer is 0.

examples.why: Both moldy buns spread at once. After minute 1 the cells next to each of them are moldy; after minute 2 the rest are. Spreading from one source and then the other would count more minutes than really pass.
The empty middle row cuts off the bottom buns, so they stay fresh forever.
There is nothing fresh to wait for, so no time is needed. It is 0, not -1.

hints: Think of the minutes as rounds. Which buns turn moldy in round 1? Which in round 2? How do the round-2 buns relate to the round-1 buns?
A bun turns moldy at minute d exactly when its shortest path (over buns) to the nearest moldy bun has d steps. That is a breadth-first search, but with many starting points.
Put every moldy bun into the queue at the start, then run BFS one level at a time. Count the levels that turn at least one bun, and at the end check whether any fresh bun is left.

explain.intuition:
Simulating minute by minute is correct but wasteful: each minute you scan the whole tray just to find the few buns on the edge of the mold. On a long winding tray, the mold advances one cell per minute for tens of thousands of minutes, and each minute costs a full scan.

Notice that the minute a bun turns moldy is its distance to the nearest moldy bun, counting steps through buns. BFS computes distances in order, and a multi-source BFS starts with all sources in the queue at distance 0, as if they were joined to one invisible super-source. Then the queue holds exactly the "front" of the mold. Processing it one level at a time is the simulation, but each bun is touched once instead of once per minute. It is the same idea as a CSS transition that ripples out from several clicked buttons at once: each ring is one tick.
steps: Scan the tray: push every moldy bun into the queue and count the fresh buns.
If there are no fresh buns, return 0.
Process the queue level by level. For each bun in the current level, turn each fresh neighbour moldy, decrease the fresh count and push it.
After each level that turned at least one bun, add one minute.
When the queue is empty, return the minutes if the fresh count is 0, else -1.
pitfalls: Running a separate BFS from each moldy bun and adding up the times, or using only the first moldy bun as the start. The sources spread together; example 1 needs 2 minutes, not more.
Counting the last level, which turns nothing, as a minute. That makes every answer one too large. Only count a level if it changed something, or subtract one at the end.
Returning -1 when there were no fresh buns at all. Nothing needs to spread, so the answer is 0.

solutions.title: Simulate minute by minute
solutions.idea: Each minute, scan the tray for fresh buns next to mold and turn them all at once. Stop when nothing changes. Correct, but a long winding tray needs one full scan per minute.

solutions.title: Multi-source BFS, level by level
solutions.idea: Start the queue with every moldy bun. Each BFS level is one minute. Each bun enters the queue once.

followups: Return, for every bun, the minute it turned moldy (or -1). What do you store instead of a single counter?
Some cells hold a cloth that delays the mold by one extra minute. Why does plain BFS stop working, and what replaces it?
